paragraphs: In 1796 the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich dismissed his assistant, David Kinnebrook, because the young man's timings of stellar transits lagged behind his own by nearly a second, a discrepancy that, at the precision the observatory demanded, could not be tolerated. The episode might have remained a footnote had the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel not come upon an account of it some two decades later. Comparing his own timings with those of colleagues, Bessel found that even skilled observers differed from one another by consistent amounts, and that practice did not remove the differences. Each observer, it seemed, carried a characteristic delay, which came to be called his personal equation.

Histories of psychology have often claimed this discovery as their own, presenting the personal equation as the first measurement of the speed of mental processes and thus as a forerunner of the reaction-time experiments of the later nineteenth century. The lineage is real, but it can obscure what the discovery meant to the astronomers themselves. For them the personal equation was not a curiosity about the mind but a practical embarrassment: it implied that the observer, long treated as a transparent window onto the heavens, was himself an instrument with errors of his own.

Their response was characteristically pragmatic. At first they sought to measure each observer's delay and subtract it, calibrating people much as they calibrated clocks. When the delays proved to drift with fatigue, with mood, and even with the brightness of the star, many observatories turned instead to devices that registered transits electrically, which narrowed, though they did not eliminate, the observer's part, and eventually to photography, which removed the eye altogether. Seen in this light, the episode may belong less to the prehistory of psychology than to a longer campaign, conducted across the sciences, to make observation independent of the particular person observing.
